strengths: Well-motivated formulation: Reconceptualizing UI-to-code generation as an interactive closed-loop visual optimization task (drafting, polishing, and editing) rather than a single-pass token prediction aligns naturally with human front-end engineering workflows and addresses rendering-dependent discrepancies.

Sound and effective RL methodology: Relative Visual Policy Optimization (RVPO) effectively addresses the non-differentiability and poor calibration of absolute VLM-based visual metrics by employing tournament-style group-wise comparisons combined with GRPO, which is clearly validated against absolute scoring and CLIP-based rewards in Section 4.3.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The paper evaluates on multiple existing benchmarks (Design2Code, Web2Code, Flame) and introduces realistic new testbeds (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench). It provides extensive human studies (Section 4.5, Table 7, Table 9), multi-evaluator cross-validation (Table 18), and comparison with modular agent baselines (Table 15).

Strong empirical performance: Despite having only 9B parameters, UI2CodeN outperforms all comparable open-source VLMs by significant margins and achieves performance competitive with, or superior to, frontier closed-source models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet) across drafting, polishing, and editing tasks.

Thoughtful diagnostic analysis: The paper includes meaningful analyses of reward hacking (demonstrating that RVPO does not exploit hard-coded absolute positioning shortcuts in Table 6), test-time scaling behavior across refinement rounds (Table 3), and microscopic oscillation phenomena during polishing (Table 17).
weaknesses: Stopping criteria and autonomous termination: While test-time scaling via iterative visual refinement is demonstrated in Table 3 and Table 16, the paper does not sufficiently formalize an automated stopping mechanism. In real-world deployment, the system must decide whether to continue polishing or terminate based only on comparing its current render with the reference, where over-refinement can lead to stylistic drift or oscillations (Section G, Table 17).

Heavy computational and rendering footprint: Continual pre-training over 20M image-code pairs followed by RL rollouts with headless browser execution (group size of 16 rollouts per prompt) represents substantial computational overhead. Full reproducibility will heavily depend on the release of training scripts, environment setups, and verifier weights.

Potential risk of template overlap: Although image hashing was applied to deduplicate crawled Common Crawl data against benchmarks, modern web designs frequently share boilerplate styling, CSS utility frameworks (e.g., Tailwind), and layout components, making subtle distribution overlap difficult to rule out entirely without deeper structural/DOM deduplication.

strengths: Sound conceptual framing: Reconceptualizing UI-to-code generation from brittle single-turn prediction into an interactive visual optimization problem with rendered execution feedback aligns naturally with real-world front-end engineering workflows.

Well-designed reinforcement learning formulation: The proposed Relative Visual Policy Optimization (RVPO) effectively circumvents the calibration and noise issues inherent in absolute VLM scoring by leveraging tournament-style pairwise comparisons and group-relative advantage estimation (GRPO).

Comprehensive three-stage training pipeline: Progressing from localized DOM-grounding continual pre-training to reasoning-augmented SFT (<think>/<answer>) and multi-aspect RL produces strong empirical capabilities in a compact 9B open-source model.

Thorough experimental validation: Evaluated across standard datasets (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code) and challenging realistic benchmarks (UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench), UI2Code^N significantly outperforms larger open-source models and matches or surpasses frontier proprietary systems.

Extensive analysis and robustness checks: The authors provide detailed ablation studies on reward formulation, training stages, reasoning traces, test-time scaling across iteration budgets, evaluator sensitivity, human-evaluator alignment, and potential reward hacking (e.g., monitoring hard-coded absolute positioning).
weaknesses: Inference and deployment constraints: The interactive visual optimization loop requires rendered browser execution and multi-round VLM calls at test time, which increases end-to-end latency and operational dependencies compared to static one-shot generation; a deeper discussion of practical deployment trade-offs would strengthen the work.

Methodological novelty of the RL objective: While the application of tournament-based relative preference to black-box visual rendering is novel in this context, the underlying algorithmic mechanics (win aggregation combined with GRPO) are largely an adaptation of established group-relative RL and tournament ranking paradigms.

Benchmark scope for UI editing: While UI drafting and polishing are thoroughly evaluated on large testbeds, the UI editing evaluation relies on a relatively modest benchmark (UIEdit-Bench, 69 samples), which leaves open questions regarding generalization to complex, long-horizon interactive editing tasks.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: Reconceptualizing UI-to-code generation from an open-loop token generation task to an interactive, closed-loop visual optimization problem reflects real-world front-end development workflows and addresses the non-differentiable nature of rendered visual execution.

Well-motivated RL algorithm (RVPO): Relative Visual Policy Optimization effectively sidesteps the noise and poor calibration of absolute scalar rewards by using tournament-style group-wise relative comparisons combined with GRPO, which is theoretically sound and empirically validated against absolute and CLIP-based rewards.

Comprehensive training pipeline: The paper details a clear three-stage progression—continual pre-training for DOM grounding, supervised fine-tuning with explicit thought/reasoning traces, and RL refinement—with thorough ablations verifying the incremental contribution of each stage.

Strong empirical results: The resulting 9B model (UI2CodeN) demonstrates state-of-the-art results across standard and newly introduced benchmarks (Design2Code, Flame, Web2Code, UI2Code-Real, UIPolish-bench), outperforming open-source baselines and rivaling top closed-source systems while being far more token- and latency-efficient than multi-agent pipelines.

Extensive validation and analyses: The manuscript includes human evaluation, thorough Human–VLM judge agreement studies (measuring Pearson/Spearman correlations, Cohen's kappa, and net-win margins), multi-run variance evaluations, reward hacking analyses (e.g., verifying hard-coded absolute positioning ratios), and investigation into test-time scaling and polishing oscillations.
weaknesses: Minor terminology inconsistency: In the Introduction and Section 2 contributions list on page 2, the method is referred to as both RVPO ('Relative Visual Policy Optimization') and VRPO ('Visual Relative Policy Optimization'); this should be standardized throughout the paper.

Heterogeneous evaluation across tasks: In the main results (Table 1), UI drafting is evaluated via thresholded o4-mini visual scoring while UI polishing is evaluated using Gemini-2.5-Pro triplet comparisons. While Appendix G provides practical justifications and cross-evaluator consistency analyses, presenting results under unified or standardized evaluators across all tasks in the main paper would make comparisons cleaner.

Sensitivity to rendering environment assumptions: While the method leverages execution feedback, web front-end rendering can be sensitive to viewport dimensions, dynamic viewport units, and external web fonts/assets. A deeper discussion on how the pipeline handles interactive states, responsive viewports, and missing remote assets would strengthen the practical scope of the system.

strengths: Compelling and realistic paradigm shift: Reformulating UI-to-code from a traditional one-shot task into an interactive, feedback-driven process (generation, polishing, and editing) closely reflects real-world frontend workflows and naturally enables test-time scaling.

Comprehensive end-to-end training recipe: The paper provides a thorough multi-stage training pipeline spanning continual pre-training with DOM referring expressions, supervised fine-tuning with structured reasoning traces, and reinforcement learning with GRPO.

Well-motivated RL reward engineering: The authors identify key limitations of CLIP similarity for UI rendering and mitigate calibration drift in VLM-as-a-judge scoring through a pairwise comparator and round-robin tournament ranking.

Strong empirical performance: For a 9B model, UI2CodeN achieves substantial gains over open-source baselines (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-72B, InternVL3-78B) and shows competitive performance with frontier proprietary models across Design2Code, Web2Code, Flame, and the proposed benchmarks.

Insightful ablation studies: The ablations systematically isolate the value of the comparator/round-robin reward design, VLM vs. CLIP rewards, and the role of real-world webpage distributions during reinforcement learning.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation for UI Editing: Although UI editing is introduced as one of the three foundational capabilities in the paradigm, Section 4 contains no quantitative benchmarks or metrics assessing edit success, precision, or instruction adherence (only qualitative demos in Appendix A.5.2).

Reliance on VLM-as-a-judge without human correlation validation: The evaluation protocol relies heavily on proprietary model evaluators (o4-mini with an arbitrary threshold of >=80 for UI-to-code accuracy, and Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing). The paper would be significantly strengthened by validating these automatic judgments against human frontend developer ratings on a representative subset.

Missing comparison against inference-time search baselines: For test-time scaling via iterative polishing (Table 2), the paper does not compare against common test-time alternatives, such as Best-of-N sampling or beam search using the trained verifier.

Context and computational overhead details: Test-time scaling requires repeated re-rendering and multi-turn visual inputs, but the paper does not discuss context length accumulation, execution failure rates during iterative loops, or wall-clock latency/FLOP overhead.

strengths: Well-motivated paradigm shift: Formulating UI-to-code as an interactive loop encompassing initial generation, iterative polishing with visual rendering feedback, and targeted editing closely mirrors actual front-end engineering workflows and naturally supports test-time scaling.

Comprehensive end-to-end training recipe: The paper provides a clear three-stage pipeline (large-scale continual pretraining with GUI referring expressions, SFT with structured reasoning chains, and GRPO-based RL directly using rendered screenshots) that balances data scale, structure, and visual fidelity.

Effective RL reward engineering: The proposed comparator-based, round-robin verifier design (Algorithms 1–3) specifically targets the known failure modes of absolute VLM scoring (calibration drift and sensitivity) and outperforms CLIP-based rewards.

Strong empirical results: The resulting 9B model substantially outpaces existing open-source VLMs across multiple benchmarks and demonstrates competitive fidelity against frontier commercial models such as Claude-4-Sonnet and Gemini-2.5-Pro.

Solid ablation analysis: Controlled experiments clearly isolate and confirm the impact of the round-robin comparator reward mechanism and the benefit of incorporating real-world web data during reinforcement learning.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation for UI Editing: Although UI editing is highlighted as one of the three foundational pillars of the proposed paradigm in the Abstract and Section 3.1, the experimental section contains no quantitative evaluation or benchmark for editing tasks (it is only demonstrated via qualitative case studies in Appendix A.5.2).

Heavy reliance on non-standard VLM-as-a-judge metrics: Established benchmarks such as Design2Code and Flame-React-Eval standardly employ objective metrics like Block-Match, element-level matching, and visual embedding similarities. In contrast, the paper evaluates all benchmarks solely via proprietary VLM judges with a threshold (e.g., o4-mini score >= 80). Complementing this with standard ground-truth alignment metrics is important for rigorous comparison with prior literature.

Potential judge alignment bias: The RL reward function trains the model to satisfy visual criteria (layout, color, typography, spacing) scored by a VLM verifier, which closely mirrors the grading criteria used by the VLM evaluators at test time. Objective code execution and structural matching metrics would help rule out reward hacking.
Incomplete repository links: The Abstract and Conclusion contain incomplete sentences ('Our code and models are available at [empty]'), leaving code/model availability unverified.

strengths: Sound conceptual framing: Re-framing UI code generation from a purely one-shot translation task into an iterative, visual feedback-driven process (generation, polishing, editing) accurately reflects real-world front-end engineering workflows.

Comprehensive training pipeline: The paper provides a thorough end-to-end recipe, spanning continual pre-training using GUI referring expression generation on ~20M vision-code pairs, supervised fine-tuning with reasoning traces (<think> tags), and GRPO-based reinforcement learning.

Well-motivated RL reward formulation: The authors identify key failure modes in standard verifiers (calibration drift across single-candidate scores and failure of CLIP similarity) and propose an effective pairwise comparator combined with a round-robin tournament across rollouts.

Promising test-time scaling results: Demonstrating consistent performance improvements over multiple iterative polishing rounds (Table 2) validates the utility of visual feedback loops at inference time.
Extensive qualitative illustrations: The appendix provides extensive and clear visual examples demonstrating full-page generation fidelity and localized editing operations.
weaknesses: Non-standard evaluation metrics without human calibration: Instead of reporting canonical benchmark metrics on established datasets (e.g., Block-Match, CLIP similarity, and element-level metrics for Design2Code; DINOv2 cosine similarity for Flame-React-Eval), the authors evaluate all tasks using an arbitrary thresholded VLM judge (o4-mini score >= 80). There is no human evaluation or meta-evaluation establishing whether this threshold and LLM prompt faithfully correlate with human design fidelity.

Complete absence of quantitative evaluation for UI Editing: UI editing is highlighted in the Abstract, Introduction, and Methodology as one of the three pillars of UI2CodeN. However, the experimental section contains zero quantitative benchmark results or baselines for UI editing, relying entirely on anecdotal qualitative samples in Appendix A.5.2.

Potential reward-evaluator alignment / Goodhart's law: The RL training is driven by a fine-tuned visual language model reward (GLM-4.5V) scored against specific rubric dimensions (layout, color, typography, spacing, details), and the evaluation is conducted using similarly prompted commercial VLMs (o4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Pro). Without independent code-level or human assessments, it is difficult to distinguish true front-end quality from optimization toward common VLM scoring heuristics.

Lack of code execution and software quality analysis: The paper evaluates solely via rendered screenshots. It lacks vital software engineering metrics such as compilation/rendering success rates, DOM complexity, CSS maintainability, or presence of non-functional artifacts.

Reproducibility and computational overhead concerns: The repository link in the Abstract is left blank ('Our code and models are available at '). Furthermore, the round-robin comparator requires O(N^2) verifier calls per training step across rollouts (N=16 yielding ~120 calls per prompt), representing substantial compute overhead that is not fully analyzed or costed.
